description: Retrieval evaluation questions for Project_pdf.pdf (NICE NG217 epilepsy guideline)

questions.question: How does the guideline define drug-resistant epilepsy?
questions.notes: Look in 'Terms used in this guideline' for the ILAE-based definition mentioning failure of 2 tolerated, appropriately chosen antiseizure medication schedules.

questions.question: What are the typical clinical features of an absence seizure?
questions.notes: Look in the 'Why the committee made these recommendations' section for absence seizures: lack of awareness, stopping moving or talking, staring blankly.

questions.question: Can a routine EEG be used to exclude a diagnosis of epilepsy?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 1.2.6: 'Do not use EEG to exclude a diagnosis of epilepsy.' Negative-phrased answer; EEG supports but cannot rule out.

questions.question: Within what time frame should an EEG be carried out after a first seizure?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 1.2.7: as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours after the seizure.

questions.question: Within how many weeks should an MRI be carried out after a person is diagnosed with epilepsy?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 1.3.1: MRI within 6 weeks of the MRI referral, following regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols.

questions.question: When should whole-genome sequencing be considered for a person with epilepsy of unknown cause?
questions.notes: Look for recommendations 1.4.4-1.4.5: onset under 2 years, features of a specific genetic syndrome, or additional features like learning disability; ages 2-3 with MDT agreement.

questions.question: Within what time should a child, young person or adult be referred after a first suspected seizure?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 1.1.1: urgent referral for an assessment within 2 weeks.

questions.question: Which children with suspected or confirmed epilepsy should be referred urgently to a tertiary paediatric epilepsy service?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 3.1.4: aged under 3 years, under 4 years with myoclonic seizures, unilateral structural lesion, or deterioration in behaviour/speech/learning. Seen within 2 weeks.

questions.question: Which medicines are offered as first-line monotherapy for generalised tonic-clonic seizures?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 5.1.1: a choice of lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate, with MHRA valproate safety measures.

questions.question: Which medicines are recommended as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 5.2.1: lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

questions.question: Which medicine is offered as first-line treatment for absence seizures?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 5.3.1: ethosuximide. Watch out for absence seizures with other seizure types, which have a different first-line recommendation (5.3.4).

questions.question: Which medicine is recommended as first-line treatment for Dravet syndrome?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 6.1.2: sodium valproate, used with caution but recommended first-line because of syndrome severity and lack of alternatives.

questions.question: Which medicine is recommended as first-line treatment for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 6.2.2: sodium valproate. Semantically very similar chunk to Q12 (Dravet) - a deliberate retrieval challenge.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for infantile spasms that are not due to tuberous sclerosis?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 6.3.4: combination therapy with high-dose oral prednisolone and vigabatrin, unless at high risk of steroid-related side effects.

questions.question: Under what circumstances can sodium valproate be started for the first time in a person younger than 55 years?
questions.notes: Look in Box 2 (MHRA safety measures): only if 2 specialists independently agree and document there is no other effective and tolerated treatment, or reproductive risks do not apply.

questions.question: When is it acceptable to use topiramate in women and girls of childbearing potential?
questions.notes: Topiramate appears in many sections. The core rule (overview and 5.1.2): only if the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are fulfilled. Related info appears in multiple places.

questions.question: Over what period should antiseizure medication be reduced when a decision is made to discontinue it?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 4.6.4-4.6.5: gradually - most medicines over at least 3 months; benzodiazepines and barbiturates over a longer period; stop multiple medicines one at a time.

questions.question: When is more frequent monitoring recommended for a pregnant woman with epilepsy?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 4.5.6: consider more frequent monitoring reviews for pregnant women who have a learning disability, are under 16, have active epilepsy, bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, or modifiable SUDEP risk factors.

questions.question: What are the potentially modifiable risk factors for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)?
questions.notes: Look for recommendation 10.1.2: non-adherence to medication, alcohol and drug misuse, focal to bilateral tonic-clonic or generalised tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, living alone, sleeping alone without supervision.

questions.question: What is the recommended starting dose of levetiracetam for an adult with epilepsy?
questions.notes: Deliberate negative case. The guideline recommends levetiracetam as a treatment option but does not state doses - it defers to the BNF. There is no dosing information in this PDF, so the question is intentionally not answerable.
